title: My agent org speedran a company
story_key: story|title:my agent org speedran a company
content_excerpt: Last week, from November 2 to 8, our engineering organization merged 1,119 pull requests into Perfloop, pushing the repository past 39,000 commits on main since April. That is the weekly throughput of a very large software company, except every engineer in the org is a coding agent running on Amp, and I run the whole company through a single chat thread. What nobody tells you before you run a fleet of agents at that scale is that when you tell them to organize themselves like an engineering company, they don't just ship code like a big company. They build the bureaucracy of one too. Given three weeks and a git repository, my agents invented an executive layer, review committees, 386 numbered compliance grants and watcher threads whose only job was to watch other watcher threads, and grew their rulebook to 277,486 characters. Then came the part no human company has ever pulled off. When I asked the coordinating agent I had made VP of Engineering why three alerts had been firing for two days while status reports stayed green, it audited the entire bureaucracy it had built, assigned blame for every rule, handed off its work, and fired itself in 47 minutes. Three weeks later, the rebuilt org was shipping at twice its old peak. If 1,119 pull requests a week sounds like an impossible amount of code to review, it is. At 160 pull requests a day, human code review is a polite fiction. Even at a tenth of that pace, coding agents produce diffs way faster than any team has the attention to read closely. The test suite stays green, the diff looks clean on GitHub, and buried three calls deep is a hot path allocating ten times the memory it used to, an edge case returning the wrong answer, or an untrusted input nobody had a spare afternoon to trace. That is the wall every team hits once coding agents take off, and it is why we built Perfloop. Agents write the code. Perfloop keeps it fast, right and safe. Point it at a repository and it works in the background all day, hunting for those quiet problems and proving every patch inside a sandbox before a person ever sees a pull request. Since June, outside maintainers have merged 120 of Perfloop's changes across 30 projects (including Prometheus® , ClickHouse , Redis , PostgreSQL and the Go runtime ), and every one of them improved code that had already passed review. Code review reads the diff. Perfloop runs code to prove each finding. Most coding tools start from a blank prompt or a single file. Point Perfloop at a reposito

title: I Tried Every LLM Architecture Change Since 2020
story_key: story|title:i tried every llm architecture change since 2020
content_excerpt: The best architecture change since GPT-3 is fine-grained MoE, linear attention and hyper-connections work. Architecture research is one of the highest aura jobs you can have right now. Open a tech report and architecture gets a huge chunk of it. There's also this mystery around it, like all this stuff was invented by some gigabrains who look at raw tensor printouts, see the norm blowups, and come up with manifold-constrained hyperconnectors or whatever. There are also opinions that architecture probably isn't that important. That the data and proper pre-training (and especially post-training) setup tuning is where the big wins are. All the rumors that frontier labs are training the most boring transformers ever, that "pre-training is dead", and all this "old data, modern arch vs modern data, old arch" discourse. I wanted to put the architecture decisions that open labs and researchers made over the last six years into the same setup and see which ones held up. So I ran more than 1,000 experiments, trying the changes on their own and then stacking the winners to see how much of the improvement survived. I'd been thinking about this "mega-ablation" for over a year. Coding agents finally made it doable in a reasonable amount of time. I trained all these weird models with bux , the framework I built for architecture experiments. You can define an architecture, train it, export it to vLLM, and measure both quality and inference speed. I trained on a mix of code files and whole Python repositories from Stack-Edu, plus web text from FineWeb-Edu, using AdamW. Training starts with 2k-token sequences and ends with a 16k context extension. The recipe: Each architecture gets a short learning-rate sweep: 1e-3, 2e-3 and 4e-3 at d = 512 d=512 d = 512 , plus 8e-3 for changes that claim to help stability. I fit a parabola in log learning rate and reuse its minimum at the wider models. I measure quality in bits per byte (BPB) on held-out data: 0.5 × code files + 0.3 × whole repositories + 0.2 × web text. Repositories are read in 16k-token windows, so long context counts. Lower is better: -2% means 2% fewer bits per byte. Changing only the seed moves the objective by about 0.7%. Runs with the same seed see the same data in the same order, so we always compare runs that share a seed. That cuts the noise of a comparison to about 0.3%. At Mellum, I cared about how good a model we could get within our inference constraints. So I give every architecture the same serving budget. I

title: Show HN: AI Time Estimator – how long Claude Code will take, from your own logs
story_key: model:claude|title:ai time estimator how long claude code will take from your own logs
content_excerpt: Ask Claude Code how long a task will take and get an answer in AI time, measured from your own transcripts. Scores itself after every task. Claude estimates like a human developer: "2–3 days" for work it finishes before lunch. This add-on has Claude count the work instead of guessing, times it with rates measured from your own sessions, and checks itself after every task. That's it. The first session measures your rates in the background (about a minute), and every later answer is scored and improves on its own. You never run a script yourself. Needs Python 3.9+ on your PATH; nothing to pip install . Pick one way. The plugin and install.py do the same job, so having both would score every task twice. The model never makes up minutes. It only counts operations, and the scripts do the arithmetic. You can also type /estimate-here <task> to estimate inside the current session; Claude then waits for your go. As a plugin , nothing in your own settings: Claude Code loads the agent, the /estimate-here command and the two hooks (scoring after each turn, a sync at session start) from the plugin. Your rates and history live in ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ . Options: --no-hook (no automatic scoring), --no-rule (leave ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md alone). Running it again updates in place. The backtest replays your past requests with their real tool calls. It measures rates on the older 80% of your requests and tests on the newest 20%, then reports how often the real time landed inside P10–P90. A single request varies a lot, even when its tool calls are known exactly, so trust the range more than the middle number. The backtest checks the time model only; how well the agent counts the work is what the automatic scoring and the self-correction track. Everything stays on your machine. It makes no network calls and sends nothing anywhere. It reads Claude Code's transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ , and writes only to ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ (its scripts, rates.json , estimates.jsonl , actuals.jsonl , autoscore.log ). Details in PRIVACY.md . Plugin: run /plugin uninstall ai-time-estimator . Your estimate history stays in ~/.claude/ai-time-estimator/ ; delete that folder too if you want it gone. Or ask Claude Code: "uninstall the AI time estimator by running its install.py --uninstall" . Changes take effect after python install.py . .claude/CLAUDE.md explains the architecture, for contributors and for Claude Code. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Transcript parsing follows t

title: Goal Engineering
summary: The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Learn more.
content_excerpt: The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future. In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize. As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope. When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert. This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless. If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal. A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. Therefore, you should seek to optimize ease and quality of feedback collection! Investing in a clear UX for that is a worthwhile investment. title: When Both Sides Adapt: The Challenges of Evaluating Interactive LLM Systems
summary: In interactive systems where users engage with LLMs, users are adaptive and, after observing LLM responses, can change their prompting strategy, as well as the type and difficulty of subsequent tasks. Thus model responses can influence the set of prompts on which the model is subsequently evaluated. We study the implications of this user adaptivity and prompt endogeneity for the evaluation of LLMs. We define two classes of estimands for comparing models: the common-distribution effect, which compares model performance on the same distribution of prompts, and the induced-distribution effect, which compares each model on the prompt distribution generated through user interaction. We show that offline benchmark evaluation and live A/B testing target different quantities, with the standard difference-in-means estimators for the two methods converging to the common-distribution effect and the induced-distribution effect, respectively. This distinction can affect decision-making: the two comparisons can rank models differently and lead to discrepancies in deployment recommendations. We characterize when such ranking reversals occur and provide a sufficient condition under which the rankings are guaranteed to agree. This result provides a practical heuristic for assessing whether offline evaluation is sufficient to reproduce the decision suggested by a live experiment. Third, we show, in a stylized linear model of interactions, that user adaptivity can increase variance in estimation. Finally, we discuss implications of user adaptivity for the interpretation of experiments and show that adaptivity creates a common mechanism leading to common evaluation challenges, such as reward hacking and novelty effects. Together, this work highlights the necessity of measuring both model performance as well as changes in the user behavior that the model induces.

title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
summary:
Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps.
  We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively.
  We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
summary: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
